history.title: Crew Launch Week 3: Where Am I Right Now?

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Responsibility. "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."

This week is about knowing your own state, so you can participate fully and mindfully.

1. Read **Where Am I Right Now?** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Word Scramble**.
3. Keep the **Four Zones, One Window** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Which Zone?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 4 is about what naming your state does NOT mean.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Emotion Zones](#sel-hub/zones?station=sel_station_crew_launch_zones). Do the one-word check-in. Then open [Window of Tolerance](#sel-hub/windowOfTolerance?station=sel_station_crew_launch_zones) and find one move that brings you back. If you have time, try [Sensory Regulation](#sel-hub/sensoryRegulation?station=sel_station_crew_launch_zones) for a move you can do at a desk.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your own check-in and reset.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Zones and the Window**.
9. Finish with the **Investigate Challenge: What Moves Me Back?**

Your commitment: this week, do a silent one-word check-in at the start of one class, and if you are not green, make one move before the lesson starts. 🚦

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Where Am I Right Now?
history.data:
## Where Am I Right Now?

**HOWL: "I take responsibility for my success as a learner."**

The Responsibility **HOWL** asks you to **participate** fully and **mindfully**. Fully means you are in the room, not just your body. Mindfully means you notice what is going on inside you and make a choice about it. You cannot do either one if you do not know where you are right now.

Your body and brain are always in some **state**. Sometimes you are calm and ready. Sometimes you are buzzing, restless, or on edge. Sometimes you are heavy, foggy, or checked out. None of these states is bad. They are information. The problem is not being in a state. The problem is not knowing it, and then trying to do hard learning from a state that cannot do hard learning.

One way to name your state is to use **zones**. Green is calm and ready. Yellow is revved up: excited, nervous, frustrated, silly. Red is overwhelmed: too much to think. Blue is low: tired, sad, bored, foggy. You do not need to be green all the time. You need to know which zone you are in so you can pick a move.

Another way to picture the same idea is a **window**. Inside your window, you can think, listen, and try things. Above the window, you are too **activated** to take in anything. Below it, you are too shut down. Every person's window is a different size, and it changes with sleep, food, stress, and what happened in the hallway two minutes ago. The goal is not a bigger window by Friday. The goal is to notice when you have left it and to know one thing that brings you back.

Here is a fictional **Crew** moment. It is Tuesday. Priya walks into Crew after a hallway argument. Her jaw is tight. Her leg is bouncing. When the Crew leader asks the group to name a zone in one word, Priya says "yellow." That one word does two things. It tells Priya what is true. And it tells the Crew leader that Priya may need a minute before she is asked to share. Nobody makes it a big deal. Priya takes three slow breaths, drops her shoulders, and by the time it is her turn to share, she is closer to green.

Naming your state is not an excuse. "I am in red" does not mean you get to leave. It means you know what you need to do first. A two-minute **reset**, a drink of water, a **sensory** move, a quiet check-in with the Crew leader. Then you come back and participate. That is the mindful part of "fully and mindfully." You are responsible for knowing where you are, and for the first move back.

This week you practice the one-word check-in. Not because Crew wants to know your business, but because knowing where you are is the first responsibility of a learner.

data.def: How your body and brain are right now: calm, buzzing, heavy, on edge.
A color word for your state: green, yellow, red, or blue.
The range of states in which you can think, listen, and try things.
Revved up. Above the window, too much energy to take things in.
Checked out. Below the window, too little energy to engage.
Noticing what is going on inside you and making a choice about it.
A short move that brings you back toward your window, like slow breaths or water.
To move your state on purpose, a little at a time.
Having to do with what your body feels: pressure, movement, sound, temperature.
To take part. Fully means your attention is in the room, not just your body.
A small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to support each other and reflect on learning. EL Education's word for advisory.
Habit of Work and Learning: a way of working that your school teaches and scores separately from academic grades. At King, the three are Respect, Responsibility, and Perseverance.

questions.question: According to the reading, what is the real problem with being in the yellow or red zone?
options: Being in those zones means you did something wrong that day
Not knowing you are there, and trying to do hard learning anyway
Those zones last all day once you are in them
Other students will notice and treat you differently
questions.correctAnswer: Not knowing you are there, and trying to do hard learning anyway

questions.question: What does "inside your window" mean?
options: You are calm because nothing stressful happened today
You are in the green zone and will stay there all class
You are in a state where you can think, listen, and try things
You are sitting quietly so the teacher does not notice you
questions.correctAnswer: You are in a state where you can think, listen, and try things

questions.question: In the reading, what did Priya's one word "yellow" do?
options: It got her excused from sharing for the rest of Crew
It told the Crew everything about the hallway argument
It let the Crew leader know she was going to be in trouble
It told Priya what was true and told the leader she might need a minute
questions.correctAnswer: It told Priya what was true and told the leader she might need a minute

questions.question: A student says "I am in red" and walks out of class. What does the reading say about this?
options: Naming a state is not an excuse; it means you know your first move back
This is exactly what naming a state is for, so it is fine
Red means you should always leave until you feel green again
The student should have said yellow so they could stay
questions.correctAnswer: Naming a state is not an excuse; it means you know your first move back

questions.question: Which is true about the size of a person's window, according to the reading?
options: It is the same for everyone in a grade
It gets bigger every week if you practice
It changes with sleep, food, stress, and what just happened
It only matters for students who have trouble with anger
questions.correctAnswer: It changes with sleep, food, stress, and what just happened

questions.question: Name your zone right now in one word, and one move you could make if you were not green.
questions.expectedAnswer: One of green, yellow, red, or blue, plus a reset move such as slow breaths, water, standing up, or pressing feet into the floor.

reflections.text: What is one move that reliably brings you back toward green? When did you last use it?

items.text: Right now I am in ____. I know because my body is ____.
When I am in yellow, one move that helps is ____.
When I am in blue, one move that helps is ____.
If I am in red, my first move is ____, and then I ____.
My window gets smaller when ____. It gets bigger when ____.
Knowing my state is my responsibility because ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Names the state | Says "fine" | Names a zone | Names a zone and one body clue |
| Has a move | No move | One move for one zone | A move for each zone I visit |
| Comes back | Uses the state as a reason to stop | Plans to return | Plans the first move back and what happens after |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: Do I have to tell the Crew why I am in yellow?
data.answer: No. The one-word check-in is the word, not the story. You can always pass.

data.question: Is it bad to be in blue a lot?
data.answer: Blue is a state, not a grade. If you notice you are in blue most days, that is worth a private conversation with your Crew leader or the school counselor. Noticing it is the responsible part.

data.question: What if my reset move looks weird?
data.answer: Most resets are invisible: slow breaths, pressing your feet into the floor, a sip of water. If yours needs space, ask your Crew leader for a signal you can use.

data.question: Can I be in two zones at once?
data.answer: Yes. Nervous and tired at the same time is common. Pick the one that is loudest and make a move for that one first.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Responsibility HOWL says you participate fully and mindfully. Knowing your state and making the first move back is the mindful part. Teachers see it as being in the room.

data.instructions: Each card locks in one idea from Where Am I Right Now? Look at the example aid, make it your own, and tell how it helps you check in.
data.sourceExcerpt: Green is calm and ready. Yellow is revved up: excited, nervous, frustrated, silly. Red is overwhelmed: too much to think. Blue is low: tired, sad, bored, foggy. Inside your window, you can think, listen, and try things. Naming your state is not an excuse.

cards.target: The four zones: green ready, yellow revved, red overwhelmed, blue low
essentialFacts: Yellow is revved up: excited, nervous, frustrated, silly.
Red is overwhelmed: too much to think.
Blue is low: tired, sad, bored, foggy.
cards.aiExample: Picture a traffic light with a puddle under it. Green go, yellow speeding up, red stop-everything-is-too-much, and the blue puddle at the bottom where energy drains out.
cards.mapping: The traffic light carries green, yellow, and red in the order of rising energy; the puddle below carries blue as the low state under all of them.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Green is like ____. Yellow is like ____. Red is like ____. Blue is like ____.
scaffoldSteps: Pick one picture that holds three colors in order.
Say the four states while looking at your picture.
coachPrompts: Which zone is hardest for you to notice from the inside?
cards.studentPrompt: Draw or describe your own picture that holds all four zones.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture help you name a zone in one word?

cards.aiExample: WINDOW = WORK ZONE. Same first letter. If I am in my window, I can work. If I am out of it, my first job is the move back, not the worksheet.

Find a word pair that keeps them together.

history.title: Investigate Challenge: What Moves Me Back?

data.title: What Moves Me Back?
data.instructions: For one school week, do a private one-word check-in at the start of three classes a day, try one reset move when you are not green, and find out which moves actually work for you. Report the pattern, not the feelings.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behavior is participating fully and mindfully. A week of check-ins turns "be mindful" into a real investigation with data the student owns, and the result is a personal reset list they can use in any class.

brief.context: Everyone has been told to "calm down" at some point. Almost nobody has been told how, or which moves actually work for them. This week you find out for yourself.
brief.role: A student investigating their own states
brief.audience: Yourself first. Then your Crew, who will hear the pattern (never the private details) in a one-minute share.
brief.drivingQuestion: Which reset moves reliably bring me back toward green, and in which situations do I need them most?
brief.seedDirection: Make a private tally card: class, one-word zone, move tried, did it help (yes, some, no). Fill it three times a day. On Friday, look for the pattern.
lockedLessonFacts: Your body and brain are always in some state, and states are information.
Inside your window you can think, listen, and try things.
Every person's window is a different size, and it changes with sleep, food, stress, and what just happened.
Naming your state is not an excuse; it means you know what you need to do first.
openQuestions: Which time of day am I most often out of green?
Which move did I think would work but did not?
What happened right before my red or blue check-ins?
stakeholders: Your Crew leader, who can help you pick moves
Your teachers, who see the result without seeing the card
criteria: At least twelve check-ins recorded over the week
At least three different reset moves tried
The report names a pattern with evidence from the tally
The report ends with a two-move personal reset list
Uses at least three glossary words correctly
constraints: The tally card is private; only the pattern is shared
No names of other people on the card
Moves must be ones you can do without leaving the room, unless your Crew leader agreed to a signal
brief.deliverable: A short pattern report (five sentences or a small chart) and a two-move reset list on an index card you keep.

parallelExample.context: A fictional student tallied for a week.
parallelExample.move: She found she was yellow almost every day after lunch and that slow breathing did nothing for her, but pressing her feet into the floor and counting the ceiling tiles did. Her reset list became: feet, then tiles. She stopped trying to breathe her way down.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows that the investigation can prove a popular move does not work for you, and that is a useful result.

supports.frameStarter: I was most often in ____ during ____. The move that worked most was ____.
frameChoices: A move that did not work for me was ____.
The thing that happened right before my ____ check-ins was usually ____.
My two-move reset list is: ____, then ____.
coachPrompts: What would you tell a sixth grader who says "I tried breathing and it does not work"?
Which of your moves could you do in the middle of a test?

data.coachHint: If a student reports "I was green all week," ask whether they checked in right after lunch or after a hard class. Green all week usually means the check-ins were done at easy times.
data.sourceExcerpt: Naming your state is not an excuse. "I am in red" does not mean you get to leave. It means you know what you need to do first. A two-minute reset, a drink of water, a sensory move, a quiet check-in with the Crew leader. Then you come back and participate.
